column9: Match each stage to what happens during it.
column14: Prophase :: Chromatin coils into chromosomes; the nuclear membrane breaks down
column15: Metaphase :: Chromosomes line up across the middle (equator) of the cell
column16: Anaphase :: Sister chromatids are pulled to opposite ends (poles)
column17: Telophase :: Two new nuclear membranes form; chromosomes uncoil
column18: Cytokinesis :: The cytoplasm divides, making two daughter cells
column28: Prophase: chromosomes become visible and the nuclear membrane breaks down. Metaphase: chromosomes line up in the middle. Anaphase: sister chromatids are pulled apart to the poles. Telophase: nuclear membranes re-form and chromosomes uncoil. Cytokinesis: the cytoplasm splits into two cells.
column29: Use the PMAT memory words from class. Each one tells what happens in that stage.

column9: Interphase is broken into which three phases?
column28: Interphase = G1 (growth 1), S (synthesis: DNA is copied), and G2 (growth 2). Prophase, metaphase, and anaphase are stages of mitosis, not interphase. G0 is when a cell leaves the cycle.
column29: Interphase is the in-between time, when the cell grows and copies its DNA but is not dividing.

column9: During which stage of mitosis do the chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell?
column15: Prophase
column28: In metaphase, spindle fibers attach to the centromeres and line the chromosomes up across the middle (equator). Prophase comes before this, and in anaphase they are pulled apart.
column29: Think about where the chromosomes have to be just before they are pulled to opposite ends.

column9: During the S phase of interphase, the cell makes a copy of all of its DNA. This process is called DNA ___.
column28: S stands for synthesis. During the S phase, DNA replication happens: every chromosome is copied so the cell will have two full sets before mitosis.
column29: It starts with r and means making an exact copy.

column9: Which structure pulls the sister chromatids apart during mitosis?
column15: The centromere
column28: Spindle fibers attach at the centromere and shorten in anaphase, pulling the sister chromatids to opposite poles. The centromere is where the chromatids are held together, not what pulls them. The nuclear membrane has already broken down, and the cell plate forms in plant cytokinesis.
column29: Think of ropes that form in prophase and attach to each chromosome.

column9: Bacteria divide by mitosis, just like human skin cells do.
column28: False. Mitosis is division of the nucleus, and bacteria (prokaryotes) have no nucleus. Bacteria divide by binary fission. Mitosis happens in eukaryotic cells, like your skin cells.
column29: Mitosis divides a nucleus. Do bacteria have one?

column9: A cat's body cells each have 38 chromosomes. A cat skin cell divides by mitosis. How many chromosomes are in **each** daughter cell?
column28: Mitosis makes two daughter cells that are identical to the parent cell, so each one has the full 38 chromosomes. The DNA was copied in the S phase first, so nothing is cut in half.
column29: Mitosis makes exact copies. Does the number change?

column9: In which part of the cell cycle does a cell spend most of its life?
column15: Metaphase
column28: Most cells spend about 90% of their time in interphase, growing, doing their jobs, and copying DNA. The stages of mitosis and cytokinesis are short by comparison.
column29: It is the stage between divisions, when the cell is just living and growing.

column9: Body cells are all the cells in your body except sperm, eggs, and the cells that make them. Body cells divide by mitosis and are also called ___ cells.
column28: Somatic cells are body cells, and they divide by mitosis. Germ cells (in the reproductive organs) divide by meiosis to make gametes.
column29: It starts with s and comes from the Greek word for body.

column9: When a human body cell goes through mitosis and cytokinesis, what is the result?
column15: Two identical diploid daughter cells
column28: Mitosis + cytokinesis turn one parent cell into two daughter cells that are identical to it and diploid (2n). Four haploid cells is the result of meiosis.
column29: Mitosis is a copy machine: how many copies, and do they keep the full chromosome number?

column9: During mitosis, spindle fibers attach to each chromosome at its centromere.
column28: True. The spindle fibers attach at the centromere, line the chromosomes up in metaphase, and pull the sister chromatids apart in anaphase.
column29: Where are the two sister chromatids held together?

column9: During interphase, the DNA in the nucleus is loose and uncoiled, like a bowl of spaghetti. What is this loose form of DNA called?
column15: Chromatin
column28: Chromatin is the loose, uncoiled DNA (with proteins) in a non-dividing cell. In prophase it coils up into chromosomes. A chromatid is one half of a copied chromosome, a centromere holds the chromatids together, and a centriole is a small structure outside the nucleus, not a form of DNA.
column29: The word sounds like chromosome, but it describes DNA before it is coiled up.

column9: What holds two sister chromatids together?
column15: The centriole
column28: The centromere is the point where the two sister chromatids are joined, making the X shape. A centriole is a separate structure outside the nucleus, not part of the chromosome. Spindle fibers move chromosomes, and the cell plate forms in plant cytokinesis.
column29: It is part of the chromosome itself: the pinched point in the middle of the X.

column9: Put the stages of mitosis in order.
column15: Metaphase
column28: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase (PMAT). Cytokinesis follows telophase to finish dividing the cell.
column29: Chromosomes have to appear before they can line up, and they have to line up before they can be pulled apart.

column9: Mitosis does many jobs for living things. Which one is **not** a purpose of mitosis?
column14: Helping a young child's body grow
column15: Replacing cells after an injury
column17: Making cells with new mixes of genes
column28: Mitosis makes identical copies, so it is used for growth, repair, and asexual reproduction. New mixes of genes come from meiosis (crossing over and independent assortment), not mitosis.
column29: Mitosis is a copy machine. Which choice would need the copies to be different?

column9: Ava scraped her knee at soccer practice. A week later, new skin has covered the scrape. Which process made the new skin cells?
column15: Mitosis
column28: Repairing damaged tissue is a job of mitosis: skin cells divide to make identical new skin cells. Meiosis makes gametes, binary fission is how bacteria divide, and crossing over happens only in meiosis.
column29: The new cells need to be exact copies of the skin cells around them.

column9: Why must the DNA be copied during the S phase **before** mitosis begins?
column14: So each daughter cell gets a full set of chromosomes
column15: So the cell has energy to build new organelles
column16: So each daughter cell gets half of the parent's DNA
column17: So the nuclear membrane is able to break down
column28: Mitosis splits the copied chromosomes between two cells. If the DNA were not copied first, each daughter cell would get only half. Copying first means each new cell gets a full, identical set.
column29: If you split one set of instructions between two cells, what would each cell be missing?

column9: Think of mitosis as a copy machine. What is being copied, and why must the copies be exact?
column14: All of the DNA, so each new cell gets every instruction it needs
column15: The cell membrane, so each daughter cell ends up the same size
column16: The spindle fibers, so each daughter cell can divide again right away
column17: Half of the DNA, so each daughter cell gets a new mix of genes
column28: Mitosis copies all of the cell's DNA (its chromosomes, the instructions). Each daughter cell needs the exact same full set to do the same job as the parent cell. Daughter cells with half the DNA and a new mix of genes come from meiosis, not mitosis.
column29: What does a cell need in order to know how to be a skin cell?

column9: Under the microscope, Maya sees a cell where the nucleolus is gone and the nuclear membrane is breaking apart. Short, thick chromosomes are scattered where the nucleus used to be. Which stage is this cell in?
column15: Anaphase
column28: The nucleolus and nuclear membrane breaking down, and chromatin coiling into short, thick, visible chromosomes, are signs of prophase. In metaphase the chromosomes would already be lined up in the middle, and in anaphase or telophase they would be moving to, or gathered at, the ends of the cell.
column29: Is the cell still getting ready, or are the chromosomes already lined up or moving?

column9: Jae sees a cell with a cluster of chromosomes at each end. A new nuclear membrane is forming around each cluster, and the chromosomes are starting to uncoil. Which stage is this?
column15: Metaphase
column28: Two clusters at the poles with new nuclear membranes forming is telophase. It is like prophase in reverse. In anaphase the chromatids would still be moving toward the poles with no new membranes.
column29: Which stage is the opposite of prophase?

column9: In an onion root tip, Saffron finds a cell where V-shaped chromatids are moving toward opposite ends of the cell. Which stage is this?
column15: Anaphase
column28: Sister chromatids being pulled apart toward the poles is anaphase. They look V-shaped because the spindle fibers pull them by the centromere.
column29: Are the chromosomes getting ready, lined up, or on the move?

column9: The chromosomes are pulled apart during metaphase.
column28: False. In metaphase the chromosomes line up in the middle. They are pulled apart in anaphase.
column29: Which stage actually separates the sister chromatids?

column9: How is cytokinesis different in animal cells and plant cells?
column14: Animal cells build a cell plate; plant cells pinch in with a cleavage furrow
column15: Animal cells skip cytokinesis; plant cells divide their cytoplasm
column16: Animal cells build a cell wall; plant cells only divide the nucleus
column17: Animal cells pinch in with a cleavage furrow; plant cells build a cell plate
column28: Animal cells divide the cytoplasm by pinching the cell membrane in the middle (a cleavage furrow). Plant cells have a stiff cell wall that can't pinch, so they build a cell plate down the center instead.
column29: Which kind of cell has a stiff wall that can't be pinched?

column9: Which events happen during **prophase**? Select all that apply.
column15: Sister chromatids separate
column28: In prophase, chromatin coils into chromosomes, the nuclear membrane breaks down, and spindle fibers form. Sister chromatids separate in anaphase, and a cell plate forms during cytokinesis in plants.
column29: Prophase is the prepare stage. Which choices are the cell getting ready, not splitting?

column9: Which events happen during **interphase**? Select all that apply.
column15: The cell grows and makes new organelles
column16: Chromosomes line up at the equator
column18: The cell makes enzymes it needs to divide
column28: Interphase is G1 (growth and new organelles), S (DNA is copied), and G2 (more growth and making the enzymes needed to divide). The nucleus dividing and chromosomes lining up are parts of mitosis.
column29: Interphase is the in-between stage: living, growing, and getting ready, but not dividing.

column9: Match each part of the cell cycle to what the cell is doing.
column14: G1 :: The cell grows and makes new organelles
column15: S :: The cell copies its DNA
column16: G2 :: The cell keeps growing and makes enzymes needed to divide
column17: G0 :: The cell is alive and working but no longer dividing
column28: G1 = growth 1 (organelles and proteins are made). S = synthesis (DNA replication). G2 = growth 2 (getting ready for mitosis). G0 = the cell has left the cycle and does not divide, like many nerve and heart muscle cells.
column29: Two of these phases are about growing. Which one comes before the DNA is copied, and which comes after? One phase is for a cell that has left the cycle.

column9: In the Time for Mitosis lab, a stage that lasts only a short time will have only a few of the counted cells in it.
column28: True. The cells in a root tip are at random points in the cycle, so a count is like a snapshot. A short stage catches only a few cells, and a long stage catches many. That is why time = (cells in stage ÷ total cells) × 720, and why interphase, the longest part of the cycle, has the most cells.
column29: Imagine taking one photo of people walking through a building. How does the time people spend in a room affect how many show up there in the photo?

column9: A skin cell and a nerve cell both came from the same fertilized egg by mitosis, so they have the same DNA. Why do they look and work so differently?
column14: Nerve cells lost some chromosomes as they grew
column15: Each cell uses (turns on) different genes from the same DNA
column16: Skin cells were made by meiosis instead of mitosis
column17: Each cell type got a different set of DNA
column28: Every body cell has the same DNA because mitosis copies it exactly. Cells become different (differentiate) by turning on different genes. A skin cell uses skin genes and a nerve cell uses nerve genes.
column29: Think of a cookbook: two cooks with the same book can make different meals by using different recipes.

column9: Mitosis is also called karyokinesis, because during mitosis only the ___ is dividing. The cytoplasm divides later.
column28: Karyon means nucleus. Mitosis divides the nucleus (karyokinesis), and cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm afterward.
column29: Which organelle holds the chromosomes?

column9: In the Time for Mitosis lab, a group counts 200 onion root tip cells, and 18 of them are in prophase. The whole cell cycle takes 720 minutes. How many minutes does prophase take? Use time = (cells in phase ÷ total cells) × 720.
column29: Divide the prophase cells by the total cells first, then multiply by 720.

column9: Which of these cells divides by mitosis?
column15: A bacterium living in your gut
column28: Cells in the stomach lining are body (somatic) cells that wear out fast, so they are replaced often by mitosis. Germ cells make sperm by meiosis, and bacteria divide by binary fission. A mature red blood cell has no nucleus, so it cannot divide at all (new red blood cells come from stem cells in the bone marrow).
column29: Mitosis divides a nucleus. Look for a body cell that has one and keeps making new cells.

column9: Put the parts of the cell cycle in order, starting right after a new cell forms.
column15: G1
column28: G1 (growth), S (DNA is copied), G2 (getting ready to divide), mitosis (the nucleus divides), then cytokinesis (the cytoplasm divides). Then the two new cells start G1.
column29: A cell has to grow and copy its DNA before it can split. Which splits first, the nucleus or the cytoplasm?

column9: Cells grow larger during telophase.
column28: False. Cells grow during interphase (G1 and G2). Telophase is when two new nuclear membranes form around the two sets of chromosomes.
column29: Which part of the cell cycle has 'growth' in the names of its phases?

column9: A human body cell divides by mitosis. Which statement is true about this division?
column14: It starts with diploid cells and ends with diploid cells
column15: It starts with diploid cells and ends with haploid cells
column16: It starts with haploid cells and ends with diploid cells
column17: It starts with haploid cells and ends with haploid cells
column28: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same: diploid (2n) in, diploid (2n) out. A human body cell with 46 chromosomes makes two cells with 46. Going from diploid to haploid is meiosis, which makes gametes.
column29: Does mitosis change the number of chromosomes?

column9: As an animal cell gets ready to divide, its two centrosomes move to opposite ends of the cell, and spindle fibers stretch out between them. Inside each centrosome is a pair of small structures. Each one is called a ___.
column28: Centrioles come in pairs inside each centrosome, outside the nucleus. In prophase the centrosomes move to opposite ends of the cell and the spindle fibers form between them. The centromere is a different structure: it is the spot on a chromosome where the sister chromatids are joined.
column29: It is not the centromere, which holds sister chromatids together. Think of the small structures in animal cells that help organize the spindle.

column9: A drug used in a lab stops spindle fibers from forming. What would happen to cells treated with this drug?
column14: The DNA could not be copied during the S phase
column15: The cytoplasm would divide before the nucleus
column16: Chromosomes could not be lined up or pulled apart
column17: Each cell would make four haploid cells instead of two
column28: Spindle fibers attach to the centromeres, line chromosomes up in metaphase, and pull chromatids apart in anaphase. Without them, the chromosomes can't be moved, so the cell gets stuck. DNA copying in S phase does not use spindle fibers.
column29: Which stages need the 'ropes' to move the chromosomes?

column9: A group counted onion root tip cells. Data table: Interphase 160 | Prophase 22 | Metaphase 8 | Anaphase 4 | Telophase 6. Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
column14: Anaphase is the longest stage of mitosis
column15: Most root tip cells are dividing at any given moment
column16: Prophase lasts almost three times as long as metaphase
column17: Telophase is the shortest stage of mitosis
column28: The more cells caught in a stage, the longer that stage lasts. Prophase has 22 cells and metaphase has 8, and 22 ÷ 8 is about 2.75, so prophase lasts almost three times as long. Anaphase has the fewest cells (4), so it is the shortest stage, not the longest, and telophase (6) lasts longer than anaphase. Only 40 of the 200 cells are dividing, so most cells are not in mitosis.
column29: More cells caught in a stage means the cell spends more time in that stage.

column9: Another group counted onion root tip cells: interphase 171, prophase 15, metaphase 6, anaphase 3, telophase 5. The full cycle takes 720 minutes. How many minutes does interphase take?
column29: Add up all the cells first. Then use (cells in interphase ÷ total) × 720.

column9: Kai counts 120 onion root tip cells: interphase 108, prophase 6, metaphase 3, anaphase 1, telophase 2. What **percent** of the cells are in mitosis (any of the four stages)?
column28: Cells in mitosis = 6 + 3 + 1 + 2 = 12. Percent = (12 ÷ 120) × 100 = 10%.
column29: Add only prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase. Then divide by the total and multiply by 100.

column9: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. After the S phase it still has 46 chromosomes, but each one has been copied (it will show up as an X once it coils in prophase). How many sister chromatids does the cell have in total?
column28: Each copied chromosome is made of 2 sister chromatids joined at the centromere. 46 chromosomes × 2 chromatids = 92 chromatids. In anaphase these separate so each daughter cell gets 46.
column29: One copied chromosome (one X) = two chromatids.

column9: Right after fertilization, a frog embryo grows by mitosis very quickly: every cell divides about once every 30 minutes. Starting from one fertilized egg cell, how many cells will the embryo have after **3 hours**? (Assume every cell keeps dividing at this rate and none die.)
column28: 3 hours = 180 minutes, and 180 ÷ 30 = 6 rounds of division. Each round doubles the number of cells: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32 → 64. This fast doubling by mitosis is how one fertilized egg starts building a whole body.
column29: First figure out how many rounds of division fit into 3 hours.

column9: Liam says, "Mitosis splits a human cell's DNA in half, so each daughter cell ends up with 23 chromosomes." What is wrong with Liam's claim?
column14: Each daughter cell actually gets 92 chromosomes after mitosis
column15: Only one of the two daughter cells gets any chromosomes
column16: Mitosis makes four cells, so each one gets about 12 chromosomes
column17: The DNA was copied in S phase, so each daughter cell gets a full set of 46
column28: Because every chromosome is copied in the S phase, mitosis can give each daughter cell a complete set: 46 in, 46 out. Halving the number to 23 happens in meiosis, when gametes are made.
column29: What happened to the DNA before mitosis started?

column9: Skin cells can be replaced quickly after an injury, but damaged heart muscle cells and brain cells usually are not replaced. What is the best explanation?
column14: Heart and brain cells divide too fast to repair anything
column15: Heart and brain cells divide by meiosis instead of mitosis
column16: Heart and brain cells have no DNA left to copy
column17: Mature heart and brain cells are in G0 and no longer divide
column28: Many mature heart muscle, eye, and brain (nerve) cells leave the cell cycle and enter G0. They are alive and working, but they do not divide, so they can't make replacements by mitosis. Skin cells keep dividing.
column29: Which part of the cell cycle means the cell has stopped dividing?

column9: Which of these are carried out by mitosis? Select all that apply.
column15: A germ cell in the testes dividing to make sperm
column16: A cut on your finger healing
column17: A lizard regrowing its lost tail
column18: A geranium cutting growing into a new, identical plant
column28: Growth (a baby growing taller), repair (a cut healing, a lizard regrowing its tail), and asexual reproduction (a geranium cutting becoming an identical plant) are all carried out by mitosis. Making sperm is different: germ cells make gametes by meiosis, so the new cells are not identical copies.
column29: For each choice, ask whether the new cells need to be exact copies of the cells that made them.

column9: Two students model mitosis with pipe-cleaner chromosomes. Which step in their model would make the two daughter cells end up with **different** chromosomes?
column14: In anaphase, both chromatids of one chromosome go to the same end of the cell
column15: In metaphase, every chromosome lines up across the middle of the cell
column16: In prophase, they twist the loose chromatin into X-shaped chromosomes
column17: In telophase, they draw a nuclear membrane around each set of chromosomes
column28: Each daughter cell should get one chromatid from every chromosome. If both chromatids of one chromosome go to the same pole, one cell gets an extra copy and the other is missing it. The other three steps are modeled correctly.
column29: Three of these choices describe the stage correctly. Which one breaks the 'one of each' rule?

column9: A cell finishes telophase normally, but cytokinesis does not happen. What would the result be?
column14: Two cells with no nucleus in either one
column15: Four haploid cells
column17: One large cell with two nuclei
column28: Telophase builds two nuclei, but cytokinesis is what splits the cytoplasm into two cells. Without it, you get one cell holding two nuclei.
column29: Mitosis divides the nucleus. Which step divides the rest of the cell?

column9: Put these events in the order they happen during cell division.
column14: A cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two
column15: Single chromatids arrive at opposite poles
column18: Chromosomes sit in one row on the equator
column28: S phase of interphase: the DNA is copied. Prophase: spindle fibers start to form. Metaphase: the chromosomes sit in one row on the equator. Anaphase: the sister chromatids separate, so single chromatids arrive at opposite poles. Cytokinesis: a cleavage furrow pinches the animal cell in two.
column29: Start with the event that happens in interphase. Then match each other event to its stage of mitosis or to cytokinesis.

column9: Why do scientists use the tip of an onion root (the meristem) to look for cells in mitosis?
column14: Onion root cells have no nucleus, so chromosomes are easy to see
column15: Root tip cells divide by meiosis, which is easier to see
column16: Root tip cells stay in G0, so they hold still
column17: The root tip is a growing region where cells divide often
column28: The meristem at the root tip is where the root grows, so many cells there are dividing. That makes it easy to find cells in every stage of mitosis. The cells do have nuclei, and they divide by mitosis, not meiosis.
column29: Where would a plant need to make lots of new cells quickly?

column9: A cell in metaphase has twice as much DNA as the same cell had in early G1.
column28: True. In the S phase every chromosome was copied, so the cell's DNA doubled. In metaphase the cell has not split yet, so it still holds both copies. The amount goes back to the G1 level only after the sister chromatids separate in anaphase and the cell divides in cytokinesis.
column29: What happened to the DNA during S phase, and has the cell divided yet?

column9: A cell entering mitosis has 8 chromosomes, and each chromosome is made of two sister chromatids. After mitosis and cytokinesis, what does **each** daughter cell have?
column14: 4 chromosomes, each made of two chromatids
column15: 8 chromosomes, each made of one chromatid
column16: 8 chromosomes, each made of two chromatids
column17: 16 chromosomes, each made of one chromatid
column28: In anaphase the sister chromatids separate, and each one becomes its own chromosome. Each daughter cell gets one chromatid from all 8 chromosomes: 8 single-chromatid chromosomes. They will be copied again in the next S phase.
column29: The chromosome number stays the same in mitosis, but what happens to the two halves of each X?
